name: PWM (Pulse Width Modulation)
summary: PWM is a way to simulate an analog output: the pin is switched on and off very fast, and the PWM duty cycle (on-time ratio) sets the average voltage.
facts: PWM output via analogWrite(pin, 0..255) on Uno (0 = off, 255 = full)
PWM pins Uno: 3, 5, 6, 9, 10, 11
PWM frequency ~490 Hz (~980 Hz on pins 5 and 6)
PWM is used to dim LEDs and set motor speed

name: Pull-up / pull-down resistor
summary: Keeps a digital input at a defined level when nothing drives it, preventing a floating, noisy reading.
facts: Uno internal pull-up: pinMode(pin, INPUT_PULLUP) (~20-50k)
With INPUT_PULLUP a pressed button reads LOW
No internal pull-down on AVR; use an external resistor

name: LED series resistor (current limiting)
summary: An LED needs a series resistor to limit current, otherwise it draws too much and burns out.
facts: R = (Vsupply - Vled) / Iled
Example: (5V - 2V) / 0.02A = 150 ohm -> use 220 ohm
Typical: 220-330 ohm on a 5V pin

name: Ohm's law
summary: The fundamental relationship between voltage, current and resistance in a circuit.
facts: V = I * R
I = V / R
R = V / I
Power P = V * I (watts)

name: Voltage divider
summary: Two series resistors split a voltage proportionally; used to scale a higher voltage down to a safe analog input level.
facts: Vout = Vin * R2 / (R1 + R2)
Used to read a 5V signal on a 3.3V ADC
Also forms the read circuit for an LDR or thermistor

name: LED polarity (anode / cathode)
summary: An LED is polarized: current flows only from anode (+) to cathode (-); wiring it backwards leaves it off.
facts: Anode = + (longer leg), cathode = - (shorter leg, flat side of the rim)
Forward voltage Vf ~1.8-2.2V (red), ~3.0-3.4V (blue/white)
Cathode connects toward ground (through the resistor)

name: Decoupling and bulk capacitor
summary: Capacitors placed across power and ground smooth voltage dips caused by sudden current draw and high-frequency noise.
facts: Decoupling: 0.1uF ceramic close to each IC's VCC/GND
Bulk: 10-470uF electrolytic on the supply rail
Essential near motors, servos, RF modules

name: Logic levels 3.3V vs 5V
summary: Boards run at 5V or 3.3V logic; feeding a 5V signal into a 3.3V-only pin can permanently damage it.
facts: 5V logic: Uno, Mega, Nano, Leonardo
3.3V logic: ESP32, ESP8266, Due, STM32, Pico
Use a level shifter or voltage divider to cross between them

name: Maximum current (pin and board limits)
summary: Each pin and the regulator can only source a limited current; exceeding it overheats or destroys the board.
facts: Uno pin: ~20mA recommended, 40mA absolute max
All AVR I/O combined: ~200mA total
5V rail (via USB): ~500mA shared
Drive motors/relays through a transistor, not directly

name: Common ground
summary: All parts of a circuit must share a ground reference; signals between two supplies need their GNDs connected.
facts: Connect external battery/driver GND to the board GND
Without common ground, signal levels are undefined
Ground = the 0V reference for all voltages

name: Transistor as a switch (NPN / MOSFET)
summary: A transistor lets a small pin current control a much larger load current, e.g. a motor, relay or LED strip.
facts: NPN BJT: base via resistor (~1k), collector to load, emitter to GND
Logic-level MOSFET (e.g. 2N7000, IRLZ44N): gate to pin, drain to load, source to GND
Load connects to + supply; transistor switches the low side
Add a base/gate resistor; add a flyback diode for inductive loads

name: Flyback (freewheeling) diode
summary: A diode across an inductive load (motor, relay coil) absorbs the voltage spike when current is switched off.
facts: Cathode (band) to +supply, anode to the switched (transistor) side
Protects the transistor from the back-EMF spike
Common part: 1N4007 or a Schottky like 1N5819

name: Voltage regulator (LDO 5V / 3.3V)
summary: A regulator turns a higher, variable input voltage into a stable fixed output (commonly 5V or 3.3V).
facts: 7805: ~7-35V in -> 5V out, needs a heatsink at high drop
Add input/output decoupling caps (e.g. 10uF + 0.1uF)

name: Logic level shifter
summary: A level shifter safely translates digital signals between 3.3V and 5V devices in both directions.
facts: MOSFET-based bidirectional modules are common for I2C/SPI
Needs both reference voltages (LV=3.3V, HV=5V) plus GND
A simple voltage divider works only one way (5V->3.3V), slowly

name: Breadboard power rails
summary: A breadboard's outer rails carry power (+) and ground (-) horizontally, while the inner columns connect 5 holes vertically.
facts: Side rails (red/blue) are continuous along the length
Inner rows: groups of 5 holes connected vertically
The center gap separates the two halves (for DIP chips)

name: Digital vs analog signal
summary: A digital signal is only HIGH or LOW; an analog signal is a continuous range of voltages.
facts: Digital read with digitalRead() -> 0 or 1
Analog read with analogRead() -> a range of values
PWM fakes analog output from digital pins

name: PWM resolution
summary: PWM resolution sets how many duty-cycle steps are available between fully off and fully on.
facts: AVR Uno: 8-bit, analogWrite 0..255
ESP32 LEDC: configurable up to 16-bit (analogWriteResolution / ledcSetup)
Uno R4 / Due: analogWriteResolution() up to 12-bit

name: ADC (analog-to-digital converter)
summary: The ADC measures a voltage on an analog pin and converts it to a number proportional to the reference voltage.
facts: Uno: 10-bit, analogRead() returns 0..1023 (0..5V)
ESP32 / Due / Pico: 12-bit, 0..4095
Uno R4: 14-bit (default 10-bit, raise via analogReadResolution)
Volts = reading * Vref / (max+1)

name: DAC (digital-to-analog converter)
summary: A DAC outputs a real, steady analog voltage (unlike PWM, which is a switched average).
facts: Uno has NO DAC (only PWM)
Uno R4: 12-bit DAC on A0
ESP32: two 8-bit DACs (GPIO25, GPIO26)
Due: two DAC outputs (DAC0, DAC1)

name: Button debounce
summary: Mechanical buttons bounce, producing several fast transitions per press; debouncing ignores changes within a short window.
facts: Typical debounce delay: 20-50 ms
Software: ignore changes until millis() - lastChange > delay
Hardware: an RC filter or a 0.1uF cap across the button

name: pinMode / digitalRead / digitalWrite
summary: pinMode configures a pin as input or output; digitalWrite drives it HIGH/LOW; digitalRead reads its state.
facts: pinMode(pin, INPUT | OUTPUT | INPUT_PULLUP)
digitalWrite(pin, HIGH | LOW) on an OUTPUT pin
digitalRead(pin) returns HIGH or LOW
HIGH = Vcc (5V or 3.3V), LOW = 0V

name: Floating input
summary: An input pin connected to nothing 'floats' and reads random HIGH/LOW from electrical noise; a pull resistor fixes the level.
facts: Cause: input not tied to a defined level
Fix: INPUT_PULLUP or an external pull-up/pull-down
Symptom: a button or sensor reading flickers randomly

name: map() and constrain()
summary: map() rescales a value from one range to another; constrain() clamps a value within min/max bounds.
facts: map(value, fromLow, fromHigh, toLow, toHigh)
Example: map(analogRead(A0), 0, 1023, 0, 255)
constrain(x, a, b) keeps x in [a, b]
map() uses integer math (truncates)

name: analogReference()
summary: Sets the top voltage the ADC maps to its maximum reading; lowering it improves precision on small signals.
facts: analogReference(DEFAULT) = Vcc (5V on Uno)
INTERNAL = 1.1V (ATmega328), EXTERNAL = voltage on the AREF pin
Never apply more than the chosen reference to an analog pin

name: tone() / noTone()
summary: tone() generates a square wave of a given frequency on a pin to drive a buzzer or speaker; noTone() stops it.
facts: tone(pin, frequency [, duration])
noTone(pin) stops the sound
Uses one hardware timer (conflicts with PWM on pins 3 and 11 on Uno)
Only one tone() at a time on AVR

name: I2C bus (Wire)
summary: I2C is a two-wire bus (data SDA + clock SCL) where many devices share the same two lines, each at its own address.
facts: Uno: SDA = A4, SCL = A5 (also broken out near AREF)
Mega: SDA = 20, SCL = 21
ESP32 default: SDA = GPIO21, SCL = GPIO22
Needs pull-up resistors on SDA and SCL (~4.7k)
Wire.begin() to start; 7-bit addresses 0x08-0x77

name: I2C pull-up resistors
summary: I2C lines are open-drain, so SDA and SCL each need a pull-up resistor to the bus voltage to return HIGH.
facts: Typical value: 4.7k (2.2k for fast/long buses)
Pull up to the bus logic voltage (3.3V or 5V)
Many breakout boards already include on-board pull-ups
One pull-up per line is enough for the whole bus

name: I2C address scan
summary: An I2C scanner probes every address and reports which devices respond, useful to find an unknown module's address.
facts: Valid 7-bit addresses: 0x08 to 0x77
Common: 0x27 or 0x3F (LCD backpack), 0x68 (DS1307/MPU6050), 0x76/0x77 (BMP/BME280)
Probe with Wire.beginTransmission(addr) + Wire.endTransmission() == 0

name: SPI bus
summary: SPI is a fast four-wire bus (MOSI, MISO, SCK, plus one chip-select per device) for SD cards, displays and sensors.
facts: Uno: MOSI = D11, MISO = D12, SCK = D13, default SS = D10
Each peripheral needs its own CS/SS line
Master drives SCK; data shifts on MOSI/MISO
Also available on the 6-pin ICSP header

name: UART / Serial (TX, RX)
summary: UART is an asynchronous two-wire serial link (TX out, RX in) used for the Serial Monitor and modules like GPS or Bluetooth.
facts: Cross-connect: device TX -> board RX, device RX -> board TX
Both ends must use the same baud rate (e.g. 9600, 115200)
Uno: 1 hardware UART on pins 0 (RX) / 1 (TX), shared with USB
Mega: 4 hardware UARTs (Serial, Serial1-3)

name: SoftwareSerial
summary: SoftwareSerial emulates an extra UART on regular digital pins when the hardware UARTs are busy or absent.
facts: SoftwareSerial mySerial(rxPin, txPin)
Reliable up to ~9600-38400 baud; unreliable higher
Only one SoftwareSerial port can receive at a time
On Mega prefer the real Serial1-3 instead

name: Serial Monitor / Serial Plotter
summary: The Serial Monitor shows text the board prints over USB; the Serial Plotter graphs numeric values in real time.
facts: Start with Serial.begin(9600) (or 115200) in setup()
Serial.print() / Serial.println() send text
Monitor baud must match the sketch's baud
Plotter graphs numbers separated by spaces/commas, one line per sample

name: WiFi (ESP32 / ESP8266)
summary: ESP32 and ESP8266 have built-in Wi-Fi to join a network (station) or create one (access point) for web/IoT projects.
facts: 2.4 GHz only (no 5 GHz)
WiFi.begin(ssid, password) to connect as a station
WiFi.softAP(...) to create a hotspot
Classic AVR boards (Uno/Nano) have no Wi-Fi; Uno R4 WiFi adds it

name: Bluetooth (HC-05 / BLE)
summary: Bluetooth links a board to a phone or PC wirelessly; HC-05/06 modules use UART, while ESP32 has built-in classic + BLE.
facts: HC-05/HC-06: UART module, default 9600 baud, 3.3V logic on RX (use a divider from a 5V TX)
ESP32 has built-in Bluetooth Classic and BLE
Uno/Nano need an external module for Bluetooth

name: Blocking vs non-blocking code
summary: Blocking code (like delay) freezes the whole program while it waits; non-blocking code keeps the loop responsive.
facts: delay() blocks: nothing else runs during it
Non-blocking uses millis() to check elapsed time
Lets you blink an LED and read a button at the same time

name: millis() vs delay()
summary: delay() pauses everything; millis() returns elapsed time so you can schedule actions without stopping the loop.
facts: millis() = ms since boot (unsigned long)
Pattern: if (millis() - lastTime >= interval) { lastTime = millis(); ... }
delay(ms) blocks for the whole duration
micros() gives microsecond resolution

name: millis() overflow / rollover
summary: millis() wraps back to 0 after about 49 days; using subtraction (now - last) instead of comparison stays correct across the wrap.
facts: Overflows after ~49.7 days (2^32 ms)
Safe pattern: (unsigned long)(millis() - previous) >= interval
Unsafe: millis() >= target (breaks at rollover)

name: Interrupts (ISR, attachInterrupt)
summary: An interrupt runs a small handler (ISR) immediately when a pin changes, without polling, ideal for encoders or fast events.
facts: attachInterrupt(digitalPinToInterrupt(pin), isr, RISING|FALLING|CHANGE)
Uno hardware interrupt pins: D2 and D3
Keep ISRs short; mark shared variables volatile; delay()/Serial unreliable inside

name: Hardware timers
summary: Hardware timers generate precise periodic events or PWM independently of loop(), used for exact timing and sampling.
facts: Uno (ATmega328): Timer0 (millis/delay + PWM 5,6), Timer1 (PWM 9,10), Timer2 (PWM 3,11 + tone)
Changing a timer can break PWM, millis() or tone() that share it
ESP32 has 4 general-purpose hardware timers

name: Polling vs interrupt
summary: Polling repeatedly checks a pin inside loop(); interrupts react instantly only when an event occurs, saving CPU for fast or rare events.
facts: Polling: simple, can miss very short pulses if loop() is busy
Interrupt: catches brief events, but the ISR must stay short
Use interrupts for encoders, fast sensors, wake-from-sleep

name: State machine
summary: A state machine models a program as a set of states and transitions, replacing tangled delays and flags with clear logic.
facts: Track the current state in a variable (often an enum)
Each loop(): act on the state, then decide the next state
Pairs well with millis() for non-blocking timing

name: volatile keyword
summary: volatile tells the compiler a variable can change outside normal flow (in an ISR), so it must be re-read from memory each time.
facts: Required for variables shared between an ISR and loop()
Prevents the compiler from caching a stale value
Multi-byte volatiles need noInterrupts()/interrupts() for atomic access

name: Integer types and overflow
summary: Integer types have fixed sizes; exceeding their range silently wraps around, causing subtle bugs.
facts: AVR: int and 'word'/'unsigned int' are 16-bit (-32768..32767 / 0..65535)
long = 32-bit, unsigned long = 0..4294967295
byte = 8-bit unsigned (0..255)
On ESP32/Due/Pico, int is 32-bit

name: setup() vs loop()
summary: setup() runs once at boot for initialization; loop() then runs forever, repeating the main program.
facts: setup(): pinMode, Serial.begin, sensor init — runs once
loop(): the repeating main logic
Together they replace a classic main() (the core adds it)

name: AVR memory (SRAM / Flash / EEPROM)
summary: AVR boards have three memories: Flash for program code, SRAM for runtime variables, and EEPROM for small persistent data.
facts: Uno (ATmega328P): 32KB Flash, 2KB SRAM, 1KB EEPROM
Flash is non-volatile (keeps the sketch); SRAM is wiped on reset
Running out of SRAM causes random crashes — watch Strings and big arrays

name: String object vs char array
summary: The String object is easy but fragments scarce SRAM; fixed char arrays are lighter and safer on small boards.
facts: String (capital S) uses dynamic memory and can fragment the heap
char buf[N] = a fixed C-string, more predictable
On 2KB-SRAM boards prefer char arrays for stability

name: F() macro and PROGMEM
summary: F() and PROGMEM keep constant strings/data in Flash instead of copying them into scarce SRAM at startup.
facts: Serial.println(F("text")) keeps the literal in Flash
PROGMEM stores constant arrays in Flash; read with pgm_read_*
Frees SRAM — important on the 2KB Uno
Mostly an AVR concern; less needed on ESP32/Pico

name: EEPROM persistence
summary: EEPROM stores small amounts of data that survive power-off, ideal for settings and calibration values.
facts: Uno: 1KB EEPROM; Mega: 4KB
EEPROM.read(addr) / EEPROM.write(addr, value); EEPROM.put/get for variables
Limited endurance: ~100,000 write cycles per cell
ESP32/ESP8266 emulate EEPROM in flash (call EEPROM.begin/commit)

name: Watchdog timer
summary: The watchdog resets the board automatically if the program hangs and stops 'feeding' it within a set time.
facts: AVR: wdt_enable(WDTO_2S); call wdt_reset() regularly
If the loop stalls past the timeout, the chip reboots
ESP32 has its own task watchdog (esp_task_wdt)

name: Deep sleep / low power
summary: Sleep modes shut down most of the chip to slash current draw, waking on a timer or pin event, key for battery projects.
facts: AVR: LowPower / sleep modes drop current toward microamps
ESP32 deep sleep: ~10uA, wake via timer or RTC GPIO
ESP32 RAM is lost in deep sleep except RTC memory
Disable unused peripherals (ADC, BOD) for the lowest draw

name: random() / randomSeed()
summary: random() returns pseudo-random numbers; randomSeed() varies the starting point so the sequence differs each run.
facts: random(max) -> 0..max-1; random(min, max) -> min..max-1
randomSeed(analogRead(A0)) seeds from a floating analog pin
Without seeding, the same sequence repeats every boot

name: Servo motor
summary: A hobby servo moves to a commanded angle using a 50 Hz PWM control signal; the Servo library handles the timing.
facts: Control signal: 50 Hz, pulse ~1.0-2.0 ms (0-180 degrees)
Servo library: myServo.attach(pin); myServo.write(angle)
Wires: signal (orange/yellow), + (red, 5V), GND (brown/black)
Power a servo from an external 5V supply, not the board's 5V, with common ground

name: DC motor and driver
summary: A DC motor draws too much current and creates noise to drive from a pin directly; a driver (H-bridge) handles power and direction.
facts: Never wire a motor straight to an Arduino pin
An H-bridge (L298N, L293D, TB6612FNG, DRV8833) sets direction and speed
Speed via PWM on the enable/PWM input
Power the motor from its own supply, share GND with the board

name: Stepper motor
summary: A stepper moves in precise fixed steps and needs a driver; bipolar steppers use STEP/DIR drivers, the 28BYJ-48 uses a ULN2003 board.
facts: NEMA17 + A4988/DRV8825: STEP and DIR pins, microstepping
28BYJ-48 (unipolar) + ULN2003 board: 4 control inputs
Holding torque consumes current even when stopped
AccelStepper library smooths acceleration

name: Relay module
summary: A relay is an electrically-driven switch that isolates the low-voltage control side from a high-voltage/high-current load.
facts: Module IN pin driven by a digital output; many are active-LOW
Opto-isolated modules separate control and load grounds
Has a built-in flyback diode across the coil
Contacts: COM, NO (normally open), NC (normally closed)

name: Analog sensor (threshold / calibration)
summary: An analog sensor outputs a varying voltage read with analogRead(); useful values come from calibrating and comparing to a threshold.
facts: Read raw with analogRead() (0..1023 on Uno)
Calibrate: record min/max, then map() to a useful range
Compare to a threshold for on/off decisions
Average several readings to reduce noise

name: Thermistor (NTC)
summary: An NTC thermistor's resistance falls as temperature rises; read in a voltage divider and convert with the Steinhart-Hart equation.
facts: NTC = resistance decreases with heat (common 10k at 25 C)
Wire it in a divider with a fixed reference resistor (often 10k)
Convert resistance to temperature via Beta or Steinhart-Hart
Read the divider midpoint on an analog pin

name: Photoresistor (LDR)
summary: An LDR's resistance drops in bright light; placed in a voltage divider it gives an analog reading of light level.
facts: Bright light -> low resistance; darkness -> high resistance
Use a divider with a fixed resistor (~10k) and read the midpoint
Not calibrated in lux — gives a relative light value
analogRead() returns higher/lower depending on divider orientation

name: Active vs passive buzzer
summary: An active buzzer beeps with just DC power; a passive buzzer needs an oscillating signal (tone()) to choose the pitch.
facts: Active: built-in oscillator, digitalWrite HIGH = fixed-tone beep
Passive: silent on DC, use tone(pin, frequency) for notes
Passive buzzers can play melodies; active ones cannot vary pitch

name: Shift register (74HC595)
summary: The 74HC595 turns 3 pins into 8 (or more, chained) outputs by shifting bits in serially and latching them to its parallel outputs.
facts: 3 control pins: data (DS), clock (SHCP/SRCLK), latch (STCP/RCLK)
8 outputs (Q0-Q7); chain via Q7' (serial out) to add 8 more
Drive with shiftOut(dataPin, clockPin, MSBFIRST, value)
Total output current per chip is limited (~70mA)

name: Multiplexing (matrix / 7-segment)
summary: Multiplexing lights one row/digit at a time very fast so the eye sees a full display, saving many I/O pins.
facts: Scan fast enough (>~60 Hz refresh) so flicker is invisible
An 8x8 LED matrix needs only 16 lines instead of 64
7-segment multiplexing shares the segment pins across digits
Often paired with shift registers or driver ICs (MAX7219)

name: RGB LED (common anode / cathode)
summary: An RGB LED packs red, green and blue chips; mixing their brightness with PWM produces colors. Wiring depends on the common pin type.
facts: 3 color pins + 1 common (anode or cathode)
Common cathode: common to GND, drive each color HIGH/PWM
Common anode: common to +V, drive each color LOW (inverted PWM)
Each color leg needs its own series resistor

name: Arduino Uno R3
summary: The classic 8-bit AVR beginner board, 5V logic.
facts: MCU: ATmega328P, 8-bit AVR @ 16 MHz
Logic level: 5V
Flash 32KB / SRAM 2KB / EEPROM 1KB
Digital 14 (PWM: 3,5,6,9,10,11), Analog 6 (A0-A5, 10-bit ADC), no DAC
I2C: A4/A5, SPI: 11/12/13, UART: 1 hardware (0/1)
LED_BUILTIN = 13

name: Uno R3 vs Uno R4
summary: The R4 keeps the Uno form factor and 5V logic but is far more capable than the R3.
facts: R3: 8-bit AVR @16 MHz, 2KB SRAM, ADC 10-bit, no DAC
R4: 32-bit Cortex-M4 @48 MHz, 32KB SRAM, ADC 14-bit, DAC on A0
R4 adds CAN bus; R4 WiFi adds Wi-Fi/BLE + 12x8 LED matrix
Both are 5V logic, same pinout

name: Arduino Uno R4 Minima
summary: A 32-bit Uno (Renesas RA4M1) keeping the Uno shape and 5V logic, far more powerful than the R3, without Wi-Fi.
facts: MCU: Renesas RA4M1, 32-bit Cortex-M4 @ 48 MHz
Logic level: 5V
Flash 256KB / SRAM 32KB / EEPROM 8KB
ADC 14-bit, 12-bit DAC on A0, CAN bus
Same Uno pinout; I2C A4/A5, no Wi-Fi (see R4 WiFi)

name: Arduino Uno R4 WiFi
summary: The Uno R4 with wireless: a Renesas RA4M1 main chip plus an ESP32-S3 for Wi-Fi/BLE, a 12x8 LED matrix, 5V logic.
facts: Main MCU: Renesas RA4M1, 32-bit Cortex-M4 @ 48 MHz
Logic level: 5V
Flash 256KB / SRAM 32KB / EEPROM 8KB
ADC 14-bit, 12-bit DAC on A0, CAN bus
Adds ESP32-S3 (Wi-Fi 2.4 GHz + BLE) and a 12x8 onboard LED matrix

name: Arduino Nano
summary: A breadboard-friendly board with the same ATmega328P as the Uno, 5V logic, in a tiny mini-USB form factor.
facts: MCU: ATmega328P, 8-bit AVR @ 16 MHz (same as Uno)
Logic level: 5V
Flash 32KB / SRAM 2KB / EEPROM 1KB
8 analog inputs A0-A7 (two more than Uno), 10-bit ADC
Digital 14 (PWM: 3,5,6,9,10,11), I2C A4/A5, mini-USB

name: Arduino Nano Every
summary: A Nano-form board with the newer ATmega4809, more memory than the classic Nano, still 5V logic.
facts: MCU: ATmega4809, 8-bit AVR @ 20 MHz
Logic level: 5V
Flash 48KB / SRAM 6KB / EEPROM 256B
Nano pinout; 8 analog inputs
More SRAM than the classic Nano (6KB vs 2KB)

name: Arduino Mega 2560
summary: A large 8-bit AVR board with many more pins and memory than the Uno, 5V logic, for big projects.
facts: MCU: ATmega2560, 8-bit AVR @ 16 MHz
Logic level: 5V
Flash 256KB / SRAM 8KB / EEPROM 4KB
54 digital (15 PWM), 16 analog (A0-A15, 10-bit ADC)
I2C: 20 (SDA) / 21 (SCL), 4 hardware UARTs, LED_BUILTIN = 13

name: Arduino Leonardo / Micro
summary: ATmega32U4 boards with native USB, so they can act as a USB keyboard or mouse (HID); 5V logic.
facts: MCU: ATmega32U4, 8-bit AVR @ 16 MHz
Logic level: 5V
Flash 32KB / SRAM 2.5KB / EEPROM 1KB
Native USB: emulates a keyboard/mouse (HID)
Serial (USB) is separate from Serial1 (pins 0/1); Micro = same chip, smaller

name: Arduino Due
summary: A 32-bit ARM board (SAM3X8E) in the Mega form factor; powerful but 3.3V logic and NOT 5V tolerant.
facts: MCU: Atmel SAM3X8E, 32-bit Cortex-M3 @ 84 MHz
Logic level: 3.3V (pins are NOT 5V tolerant — 5V can destroy them)
Flash 512KB / SRAM 96KB
ADC 12-bit, two DAC outputs (DAC0, DAC1)
54 digital pins, 12 PWM, 4 UARTs

name: Arduino Pro Mini
summary: A minimal ATmega328P board without USB; needs an FTDI/USB-serial adapter to program. Comes in 5V and 3.3V variants.
facts: MCU: ATmega328P (same core as Uno)
Two variants: 5V/16 MHz and 3.3V/8 MHz
Flash 32KB / SRAM 2KB / EEPROM 1KB
No onboard USB — program via an external FTDI adapter
Very compact; popular for battery / embedded builds

name: ESP32 DevKit v1
summary: A dual-core 3.3V Wi-Fi + Bluetooth board widely used for IoT; powerful but its pins are 3.3V only.
facts: MCU: Espressif ESP32 (Xtensa dual-core LX6) @ up to 240 MHz
Logic level: 3.3V (NOT 5V tolerant)
Wi-Fi 2.4 GHz + Bluetooth Classic + BLE
Analog inputs: up to 18 ADC channels, but ADC2 is unusable while Wi-Fi is on (~8-15 usable in practice)
ADC 12-bit (0..4095), two 8-bit DACs (GPIO25/26)
Default I2C: GPIO21 (SDA) / GPIO22 (SCL), LED_BUILTIN = 2

name: ESP8266 (NodeMCU / Wemos D1)
summary: A low-cost 3.3V Wi-Fi board; single-core, fewer pins than the ESP32, with only one limited analog input.
facts: MCU: ESP8266 @ ~80 MHz (can run 160 MHz)
Logic level: 3.3V (NOT 5V tolerant)
Wi-Fi 2.4 GHz (no Bluetooth)
Single analog input A0, 0-1V max at the chip (NodeMCU board has a divider to ~3.2V)
I2C is software/bit-banged on chosen GPIOs

name: STM32 Blue Pill (F103C8)
summary: A cheap, fast 32-bit ARM board (STM32F103C8T6); 3.3V logic with some 5V-tolerant pins.
facts: MCU: STM32F103C8T6, ARM Cortex-M3 @ 72 MHz
Logic level: 3.3V (some pins are 5V-tolerant)
Flash 64KB / SRAM 20KB
ADC 12-bit, multiple timers, USART/SPI/I2C
Usually flashed via ST-Link or USB-serial bootloader

name: Raspberry Pi Pico
summary: A dual-core ARM Cortex-M0+ board (RP2040) with lots of RAM; 3.3V logic, programmable I/O (PIO).
facts: MCU: RP2040, dual-core Cortex-M0+ @ 133 MHz
Logic level: 3.3V (NOT 5V tolerant)
264KB SRAM, 2MB onboard flash
3 analog inputs (12-bit ADC)
Unique PIO state machines; Pico W variant adds Wi-Fi

name: Uno vs Mega vs Nano
summary: Three 5V AVR boards: the Uno is the standard, the Mega adds many pins and memory, the Nano is a tiny breadboard version of the Uno.
facts: Uno: 14 digital, 6 analog, 2KB SRAM, 1 UART, ATmega328P
Mega: 54 digital, 16 analog, 8KB SRAM, 4 UARTs, ATmega2560
Nano: same ATmega328P as Uno but 8 analog inputs, smaller mini-USB form
All three are 5V logic, 8-bit AVR @ 16 MHz

name: 5V vs 3.3V boards
summary: Boards run their I/O at either 5V or 3.3V; mixing them carelessly can destroy a 3.3V input fed a 5V signal.
facts: 5V logic: Uno, Mega, Nano, Leonardo (AVR)
3.3V logic: ESP32, ESP8266, Due, STM32, Pico
Connecting a 5V output to a 3.3V-only input can permanently damage it
Cross levels with a level shifter or (5V->3.3V) a voltage divider

name: BME280 vs BMP280 (board sold as BME280 carrying a BMP280)
summary: A board sold as BME280 can carry a BMP280 instead: same pinout, same I2C addresses, but no humidity sensor at all.
facts: Read the chip-id register 0xD0: 0x60 = BME280, 0x58 = BMP280
Board silkscreen GY-BMP280-3.3, also silkscreened HW-611: a BMP280 module
A BMP280 has NO humidity sensor, so humidity can never work on it
Both use I2C address 0x76 or 0x77 and the same pinout, so the swap is invisible from the wiring
Adafruit_BME280 library: begin() checks the chip ID equals 0x60 and returns false otherwise, so a BMP280 (0x58) fails begin() outright rather than silently reading humidity as 0
If the chip is a BMP280, use a BMP280 library and drop humidity from the sketch

name: MPU9250 vs MPU6500 (board sold as MPU9250 carrying an MPU6500)
summary: A board sold as MPU9250 can carry an MPU6500 instead: same pinout, same I2C addresses, but no magnetometer at all.
facts: Read the WHO_AM_I register 0x75: 0x71 = MPU9250, 0x70 = MPU6500
An MPU9250 is an MPU6500 plus an AK8963 magnetometer; an MPU6500 has NO magnetometer
Both use I2C address 0x68 or 0x69 and the same pinout, so the swap is invisible from the wiring
Without a magnetometer there is no heading reference, so yaw drifts in any 9-DOF orientation fusion
Reported figure: around 25 percent of boards sold as MPU9250 carry an MPU6500
If the chip is an MPU6500, use a 6-axis library and drop the compass, or add a separate magnetometer such as an HMC5883L

name: Counterfeit DS18B20 (clone sold as a Maxim DS18B20)
summary: Most DS18B20 parts sold today are clones rather than genuine Maxim silicon: they read the right ballpark but miss the datasheet accuracy and often fail in parasite power mode.
facts: Read the 1-Wire ROM address: a pattern 28-xx-xx-xx-xx-00-00-xx indicates a clone, because the genuine ROM is a 48-bit counter whose high bytes are still zero
Most clones leave reserved byte 6 of the scratchpad at a value the datasheet forbids
Known clone symptoms: parasite power fails, higher noise, temperature offset beyond the advertised plus/minus 0.5 C band, and unusable EEPROM
The OneWire example sketches already print the ROM address, so this check needs zero extra library
A clone still reports a temperature: suspect it for accuracy and parasite power, rather than for a broken part

name: OLED sold as SSD1306 driven by an SH1106 controller (2-pixel shift)
summary: OLED modules that look identical can carry either an SSD1306 or an SH1106 controller; driving an SH1106 with an SSD1306 library shifts the whole image by 2 pixels.
facts: The SH1106 has 132 columns of RAM but only 128 visible, and the visible area starts at column 2
An SSD1306 library writes from column 0, so on an SH1106 the first 2 pixels of every page fall outside the visible window: the image shifts and the edge shows stray pixels
Rule of thumb: a 0.96 inch module is usually SSD1306, a 1.3 inch module is almost always SH1106
The controller marking is printed on the small IC on the back of the module
Fix without rewiring: use the Adafruit SH110X library, or declare SH1106 in U8g2, which apply the column offset

name: GY-271 silkscreened HMC5883L carrying a QMC5883L
summary: A GY-271 board silkscreened HMC5883L often carries a QMC5883L from a different maker: different I2C address and a completely different register map, so an HMC5883L library reads zeros.
facts: Scan the I2C bus: address 0x1E means HMC5883L, address 0x0D means QMC5883L
The GY-271 silkscreen frequently says HMC5883L even when the chip on it is a QMC5883L, so the printed marking cannot be trusted here
The two register maps differ entirely, including where the x, y and z bytes sit, so an HMC5883L library returns zeros on a QMC5883L
Fix without rewiring: keep the board and switch to a QMC5883L library
Both parts measure the same quantity, so once the matching library is used the board works as a compass

name: I2C LCD backpack carrying a PCF8574 (0x27) or a PCF8574A (0x3F)
summary: Visually identical I2C LCD backpacks ship with either a PCF8574 or a PCF8574A expander: one answers at 0x27, the other at 0x3F, so a sketch hard-coded to the wrong address drives a lit but blank panel.
facts: Scan the I2C bus: a backpack built on a PCF8574 answers at 0x27, one built on a PCF8574A answers at 0x3F
Both variants drive the same 1602 or 2004 panel through the same LiquidCrystal_I2C library, so only the address given to the constructor changes
The A0, A1 and A2 solder pads move the address inside 0x20-0x27 for a PCF8574 and inside 0x38-0x3F for a PCF8574A
Read the marking on the expander chip itself: PCF8574T and PCF8574AT are one letter apart
A lit backlight showing a row of solid blocks points at the address or at the contrast trimmer rather than at a broken panel

name: Board silkscreened ADS1115 carrying an ADS1015 die
summary: Boards printed ADS1115 are shipped with ADS1015 silicon, which shares the same I2C register map and answers every transaction with plausible numbers. Only the resolution betrays it: the four low bits stay at zero, so readings move in jumps of 16.
facts: Print raw counts from a single-ended read on a slowly varying input: ADS1015 silicon returns values spaced 16 apart, such as 26352, 26368, 26384, while genuine ADS1115 silicon moves count by count
At gain plus or minus 0.256 V an ADS1115 step equals 7.8125 microvolts; a substituted die yields about 125 microvolts per observable step, a sixteen times coarser grain
Throughput separates the two dies as well: ADS1115 tops out at 860 samples per second, ADS1015 at 3300. Request the maximum data rate and time the conversions
Chip top marking gives a hint only: BOGI marks ADS1115 silicon and BRPI marks ADS1015, but the ADS1115_WE README shows a board whose marking is plainly wrong, so trust the measurement over the label
The swap runs in both directions, ADS1015 dies on ADS1115 boards and ADS1115 dies on ADS1015 boards, so measure rather than assume

name: DHT20 wearing the DHT housing but speaking I2C at 0x38
summary: The DHT20 ships in the familiar DHT-series housing and four-pin footprint, yet it holds an AHT20 die and talks over I2C at address 0x38 instead of the single-wire timing protocol. A DHT library therefore drives the wrong bus entirely and reads NaN forever on a healthy part.
facts: Run an I2C scan before anything else: a device answering at 0x38 is AHT20 class and needs a DHT20 or AHT driver, whatever the housing suggests
Adafruit product 5183 states it plainly: the part looks like a DHT11 or DHT22, inside is the AHT20, and the interface is plain I2C at address 0x38, which cannot be changed
A DHT library drives the single-pin timing protocol and receives nothing, so readTemperature and readHumidity return NaN forever while the part answers an I2C scan normally
The Arduino Sensor Kit replaced its DHT11 module with a DHT20 I2C module, so kit documentation and older tutorials describe two different buses for parts that look the same

name: APDS-9960 clone answering 0xA8 at the ID register
summary: Widely sold APDS-9960 breakouts carry silicon returning 0xA8 from the ID register where Broadcom parts return 0xAB. Every mainstream library hard-codes 0xAB, so begin() rejects a module that acknowledges normally on the bus and is otherwise sound.
facts: Read register 0x92 at I2C address 0x39: genuine silicon answers 0xAB, the clone answers 0xA8. A scan showing 0x39 present while begin() refuses the part is the exact signature
SparkFun_APDS9960.h defines APDS9960_ID_1 as 0xAB; changing that single constant to 0xA8 makes the SparkFun examples run on the clone

On 0xA8 silicon the ENABLE register at 0x80 powers up holding 0x09, which leaves the gesture engine idle. Writing 0x7F to 0x80 turns the gesture modes on, but the same report warns this DISABLES the RGB colour detector, so pick one function or the other
The official Arduino_APDS9960 library still hard-codes 0xAB, so Nano 33 BLE gesture examples stop at begin() on these boards until the check accepts both identifiers
The 0xA8 parts drive the interrupt pin unreliably, so poll the gesture FIFO rather than wait on that line

name: K-type thermocouple boards mixing MAX6675 and MAX31855
summary: Cheap red K-type thermocouple breakouts carry either a MAX6675 or a MAX31855, sometimes on a layout drawn for the other part. A MAX6675 layout ties the thermocouple negative lead to ground, which a MAX31855 reports as a permanent short-to-ground fault.
facts: Measure the resistance between the thermocouple minus pad and GND: a MAX6675 layout connects them on purpose, and that same connection makes a MAX31855 raise its short-to-ground fault forever
MAX31855 fault bits: D0 open circuit, D1 short to ground, D2 short to supply, D16 any fault. A short-to-ground report with a known-good probe attached points at the board layout, not at the wiring

A chip whose three marking lines read M31855K, 1424A2 and +780AB returns a frozen cold junction of 128.00 and a thermocouple reading of 0.00 whatever probe is attached; several buyers saw it across sellers
The two parts differ on the wire: MAX6675 sends 16 bits, MAX31855 sends 32, so a MAX6675 library on a MAX31855 misreads in silence
Silkscreens sometimes print both part numbers, and the MAX31855 is marketed as a MAX6675 upgrade, so the printed name settles nothing

name: MCP4725 factory address variants under one silkscreen
summary: The MCP4725 exists in four factory variants whose base address is burned into the die, while the module silkscreen only ever says MCP4725. Code written for one breakout answers nothing on another even though a bus scan shows a live device.
facts: Scan the bus and match the address to the variant table: MCP4725A1 sits at 0x62 and 0x63, A2 at 0x64 and 0x65, A3 at 0x66 and 0x67
The Adafruit breakout is the A1 variant and documents 0x62 as its default, 0x63 with A0 tied high, so hardcoding 0x62 from that tutorial fails on a generic board while a scan still finds a device
The variant cannot be read over the bus: there is no identifier register, so a scan plus the table, or the package marking under magnification, are the only routes
The variant suffixes A0 to A3 collide by name with the chip A0 address pin, and that pin only shifts the address by one inside a variant pair rather than selecting the variant
This is a factory variant rather than a counterfeit: the die is genuine and the datasheet describes every address, but the module never prints which one it carries

name: MAX30100, MAX30102 and MAX30105 on identical purple breakouts
summary: Three different pulse oximeter dies ship on visually identical purple breakouts, answer at the same bus address and are listed interchangeably by sellers, yet they need different libraries. The wrong driver initialises without complaint and returns unusable data.
facts: All three parts answer at address 0x57, so a bus scan proves presence and never identity
Read register 0xFF, the part identifier: 0x11 means MAX30100, while 0x15 means MAX30102, MAX30105 or MAX30101, so 0x15 narrows the choice without settling it alone
Register 0xFE holds the revision identifier and separates production runs once the family is known
A MAX30100 driven by a MAX30102 library, or the reverse, starts up without complaint and returns unusable data, because the register maps diverge although the address matches

name: Board labelled Si7021 carrying an HTU21D or SHT21 die
summary: The generic GY-21 breakout ships indifferently with a Si7021, a Si7020, a TE HTU21D or a Sensirion SHT21, all at the same bus address and all answering the same measurement commands. The swap stays invisible until a Si7021 driver tries to identify the part at init and aborts.
facts: Send command 0xFC 0xC9 and read the electronic identifier: the first byte returned is SNB_3, and Silicon Labs maps it to 0x15 for a Si7021 and 0x14 for a Si7020
An SNB_3 of 0x32 means the die is an HTU21D or an SHT21 rather than a Silicon Labs part, which is the whole substitution in one byte
All four parts answer at address 0x40, so an address scan separates nothing and only the electronic identifier settles it
The checksum byte is mandatory on the identifier reads and optional on measurement commands, so a driver that skips those clock cycles fails identification even on a genuine part
ESPHome documents the case verbatim: some boards may be mislabeled, and trying the HTU21D model is the suggested remedy on bus errors

name: Si24R1 clones and remarked dies sold as nRF24L01+
summary: Modules identical to an nRF24L01+ carry either a NanJing Si24R1 register-level clone or a remarked die with Nordic markings. Mixed links pair, then drop packets as soon as auto acknowledge or dynamic payloads are enabled.
facts: Write 1 into bit 0 of RF_SETUP at register 0x06 and read it back: a genuine nRF24L01+ ignores that bit and returns 0, a Si24R1 uses it as RF_PWR bit 0 and returns 1
The Si24R1 firmware reproduces a typo from the original nRF24L01 datasheet, so its auto acknowledge misbehaves against a genuine part
Remarked dies reverse the NO_ACK bit once EN_DPL is set, so a link that works with fixed payloads breaks the moment dynamic payload length is turned on
Power-down current separates them without any bus transaction: genuine parts draw well under a microamp, measured fakes draw several
Package marking: genuine Nordic dies carry a square index in the top-left corner, the remarked ones a circle with misaligned text

name: ST7735B, ST7735R and ST7735S sold interchangeably
summary: Modules advertised as ST7735 carry several controllers and panel binnings needing different init sequences, memory offsets and colour filter order. The plastic tab colour used to hint at the binning and no longer does.
facts: Image two pixels right and one pixel low with a garbage column on the opposite edge: the panel is the green tab binning and needs colstart 2 and rowstart 1, where the red tab binning uses 0 and 0
On a 1.44 inch 128 by 128 panel the same symptom needs colstart 2 and rowstart 3, and the row offset flips between 3 and 1 with rotation
Red and blue swapped on a 1.8 inch panel: the black tab binning issues MADCTL 0xC0 and uses an RGB colour filter where the others use BGR
A 0.96 inch 160 by 80 panel needs colstart 24, and its plug-in variant needs 26 with inversion on and off exchanged, which shows as a full photo negative image
A panel staying black under every initR variant is ST7735B silicon and needs the separate initB path, an entirely different command sequence

name: PMS5003 internal revision shipped under identical markings
summary: Plantower shipped a PMS5003 with a new internal board and MCU while keeping the casing, the part number and the markings unchanged. The new units divide the smallest particle bin by three and read low indoors, so two identical-looking sensors disagree with no error and no flag.
facts: Use data the sensor already reports: divide the count of particles at or above 0.3 um by the count at or above 0.5 um. A ratio under 2 indicates the new hardware, over 3 the old
The ratio works because Plantower divided the 0.3 um bin counts by three in the new design
The low bias appears below 16 micrograms per cubic metre of raw PM2.5 and reaches half or more, while the two designs agree above that, so a bench check at high concentration hides it
Roughly one tenth of the PurpleAir fleet was affected, and those units can be corrected with a linear relationship rather than replaced
This is the maker changing the silicon under an unchanged part number, not a third party counterfeit, which is why no marking betrays it

name: VL53L0X and VL53L1X share one silkscreen and one address
summary: GY-530 and GY-53 carriers ship with either a VL53L0X or a VL53L1X, both answering at 0x29 behind an identical footprint. Their register maps are incompatible, so a VL53L0X driver talking to a VL53L1X hangs or ranges garbage.
facts: Read 8-bit register 0xC0, the model identifier: a VL53L0X answers 0xEE, which is exactly what the Pololu driver checks at init
Read 16-bit register 0x010F instead: a VL53L1X answers 0xEA, and a 16-bit read across 0x010F and 0x0110 gives 0xEACC
VL53L0X uses 8-bit register addressing while VL53L1X, VL53L3CX and VL53L4CD use 16-bit, so probing with the wrong width can hang the bus master
Both parts sit at address 0x29 by default, so the bus scan is never the diagnostic here, the identifier read is
Tasmota states it plainly: a driver cannot identify which of the two it talks to, and the user must select the family by hand

name: GY-521 marked MPU-6050A carrying a different InvenSense die
summary: A widespread batch of GY-521 boards is silkscreened MPU-6050A but the die answers 0x98 at its identity register, the signature of an ICM-20689. Libraries reject the board at connection test, and patched ones then write to offset registers that live elsewhere.
facts: Read register 0x75, the identity register: a genuine MPU-6050 answers 0x68, the relabelled parts answer 0x98
0x98 is impossible on a genuine part, because the MPU-6050 map fixes bit 0 and bit 7 of that register at zero, so any value with bit 7 set proves a different die
0x98 is the documented identity of the ICM-20689, which is the part actually mounted on those boards
Libraries compare the masked value, bits 6 down to 1: genuine gives 0x34, and the ElectronicCats library was patched to accept 0x4C too, the masked form of 0x98
Beyond identity the offset registers are relocated, so calibration sketches written for an MPU-6050 write to the wrong addresses in silence

name: INA219 and INA226 share an address block and a shape
summary: Both current monitors occupy the same address block on interchangeable breakouts, but their register maps differ. An INA219 driver pointed at an INA226 returns plausible numbers off by a fixed factor, which is worse than returning nothing.
facts: Read register 0x00 after power-up: an INA219 resets to 0x399F, an INA226 resets to 0x4127, which separates the two on its own
An INA226 answers 0x5449 at register 0xFE and 0x2260 at register 0xFF; the INA219 map stops at 0x05 and has no equivalent

Shunt voltage steps are 10 microvolts on the INA219 against 2.5 on the INA226, and bus voltage 4 millivolts against 1.25, so the wrong driver scales readings by four and by 3.2 while staying believable
An INA219 needs its calibration register at 0x05 programmed before current and power mean anything, while an INA226 converts straight out of reset

name: Ai-Thinker Ra-01 family mixes SX127x and SX126x radios
summary: Ra-01 and Ra-02 carry an SX1278 and Ra-01H an SX1276, but Ra-01S carries an SX1268 and Ra-01SH an SX1262, a wholly different command architecture on the same footprint. An SX127x library aborts because the register it probes is absent.
facts: SX127x drivers probe RegVersion at 0x42 and expect 0x12; SX126x parts are opcode driven with no register there, so begin returns zero and the board looks absent
Ai-Thinker documents the split: Ra-01 and Ra-02 hold an SX1278, Ra-01H an SX1276, Ra-01S an SX1268 and Ra-01SH an SX1262

RegVersion cannot separate an SX1276 from an SX1278, since Semtech documents them as identical apart from the supported radio bands, so a board matched for 433 MHz driven at 868 transmits outside its network
RadioLib needs a different class per family, and an Ra-01SH marked LLCC68 has to be driven through the SX1262 class
Parts marked LLCC68 support spreading factors 5 to 11 only, where SX1262 and SX1268 reach 12, so a spreading factor of 12 fails to configure in silence

name: Six-digit TM1637 boards address digits in two reversed blocks
summary: Four-digit and six-digit TM1637 boards share the chip, the two-wire interface and the product name, but the six-digit board wires its digits as two reversed groups of three. Writing 123456 prints 321654.
facts: Reproducible test: write 123456. A six-digit board renders 321654, because the two blocks of three digits are internally reversed
The remedy is a digit remap table, not a different library call; libraries supporting both ship that map explicitly
Clone boards omit the 10 kilohm pull-ups the TM1637 datasheet calls for on the data and clock lines; a 1 kilohm pull-up from data to 3.3 volts fixes the corrupted transfers
The bit delay defaults to 10 microseconds: lowering it to zero works on some boards and corrupts data on pull-up-less clones, because the data line never reaches a valid high
Two four-digit variants also circulate under one name, one with a decimal point per digit and one with a colon in the middle; the colon is a segment bit of the second digit, not a separate device

name: TM1638 boards needing different driver classes
summary: Several boards carry a TM1638 and are all sold as TM1638 module, yet one drives a common cathode display with eight buttons and another a common anode display with a sixteen key pad. One class on the other board garbles the digits.
facts: Three boards circulate: one with eight digits, eight red lights and eight buttons, one common anode with sixteen keys as a four by four pad, and one with eight bi-colour lights
Common anode transposes the digit and segment axes, so the sixteen key board needs its own driver class rather than a parameter
Key numbering on the eight button board is interleaved rather than sequential, which reads as random buttons until the mapping is applied
The sixteen key board returns its keys as a sixteen bit value through a dedicated method, which the eight button read cannot express
The eight button board has no short circuit diodes, so pressing more than two keys at once returns wrong results by design

name: The 28BYJ-48 gearbox ratio differs from the printed figure
summary: The stepper shipped with every ULN2003 board is specified as a 64 to 1 reduction but measures 63.68395 to 1, so step counts taken from the marking accumulate a positional error. Two coil voltages also ship in the same blue can.
facts: The measured gearbox is 63.68395 to 1, giving 2038 full steps per output turn rather than the 2048 the nominal figure predicts, so about half a percent of drift accumulates every revolution
The stride angle printed on the label derives from the nominal figure and inherits the same error
Two coil voltages share an identical blue housing: measure the phase resistance, the five volt unit is specified near 50 ohms while twelve volt units measure several times that
The harm is asymmetric: a twelve volt unit driven at five volts merely loses torque, a five volt unit driven at twelve overheats
Pin order does not follow the connector order: the Arduino Stepper constructor must be given in one, in three, in two, in four, or the shaft vibrates instead of turning

name: Common INA3221 breakouts bridge all three inputs to one pin
summary: The widely cloned INA3221 breakout ties its three positive inputs together to a single supply pin, so the three channels cannot watch three independent rails. The chip is genuine; the board removes the very feature it is bought for.
facts: Reproducible check without opening anything: feed three different voltages and read the three bus voltage registers. Identical readings across channels prove the bridge
On the affected layout the three positive inputs are bridged to one supply pin and every ground is common, so the channels necessarily share one rail
Purple and black boards are electrically identical; on the purple ones the traces are easier to follow, which is how owners check their own revision
The documented remedy is cutting the traces on both faces where the shunts meet the shared pours, then wiring separate connectors
The default shunt on these boards is 0.1 ohm, and reworking it to 0.01 for higher current changes the scaling the software must apply

name: MQ-135 parts per million rest on a reference nobody measures
summary: The MQ-135 is one tin dioxide element whose datasheet reference point is defined in ammonia, not in carbon dioxide, and must be measured on each individual unit. The library everyone copies ships a placeholder reference, so its parts per million figure has no referent.
facts: The datasheet defines the reference resistance in clean air at 100 parts per million of ammonia, at 20 degrees and 65 percent humidity, with a 20 kilohm load, so every figure is a ratio against an ammonia anchor rather than a carbon dioxide one
The widely copied library hardcodes a reference of 76.63 and a load of 10 kilohms, half the datasheet standard, and its own source carries the author note doubting the datasheet
That reference varies unit to unit even within one batch, so it has to be measured per element rather than copied
One element responds to ammonia, nitrogen oxides, alcohol, benzene, smoke and carbon dioxide at once, so a single resistance cannot attribute the change to any one of them
The baseline constant 397.13 is a frozen 2014 outdoor figure, and ambient carbon dioxide has since moved past 420, so even a calibrated unit drifts against its own anchor

name: MFRC522 clones announce themselves in the version register
summary: A large share of RC522 breakouts carry a Fudan FM17522 die or an outright counterfeit instead of the NXP part on the listing. The reference library already names the part for you, but only in the one sketch nobody runs first.
facts: Run the firmware_check sketch: it reads the version register at 0x37 and prints the raw byte. Genuine NXP parts answer 0x90, 0x91 or 0x92
A version byte of 0x88 is a Fudan FM17522 clone, which the library source labels as such and prints as clone; a byte of 0x12 prints as counterfeit
A reading of 0x00 or 0xFF is a wiring fault rather than a fake, and the library says so: check the SPI link before blaming the die
Any other value prints as unknown, and if that reading is permanent rather than intermittent the board is fake or defective
The self test compares 64 buffer bytes against a per-version table and gives up for any version outside the four known ones, so a clone with an unlisted version cannot be validated at all

name: The ZS-042 board charges a cell that must never be charged
summary: The DS3231 die holds no charger at all: the charging path is drawn by the module designer, from the supply through a 200 ohm resistor and a diode into the cell holder. It was sized for a rechargeable cell, and the boards circulate with primary cells fitted.
facts: Measurement that decides it: power the module from 5 volts and meter the coin cell in place. Above 3.3 volts means the charging path is live and the cell is being pushed
The path is external to the chip, a 200 ohm resistor plus a diode between the supply and the cell holder, which is why the DS3231 datasheet says nothing about it
On a 5 volt rail roughly 5 milliamps flow into a chemistry rated for zero charging current; the cell swells, vents or bursts, and a bulging cell should be discarded
Remedy: unsolder either the 200 ohm resistor or the diode, taking care NOT to cut the track that runs from the cell to pin 14 of the DS3231
Running the board from 3.3 volts leaves no headroom past the diode drop, so no charging occurs without any modification at all

name: Motor Shield V2 answers a second address nobody assigned it
summary: The shield replies to the address set by its jumpers and also to the all-call address, which is enabled at power-up and which no jumper controls. Anything else parked there collides with a shield that appears, by its silkscreen, to be elsewhere.
facts: Run a bus scanner with the shield fitted: it reports the shield twice, once at its jumper address and once at the all-call address 0x70
The controller datasheet states the hazard itself: the default all-call address must not be used as a regular slave address, because it is enabled at power-up
The board vendor documents the consequence in its own answers: display backpacks defaulting to 0x70 clash with the shield until re-addressed
Remedy: re-address the other device, or clear the all-call bit, bit 0 of the mode register, after init; its power-up default is 1

name: LSM303 names five chips with three incompatible register maps
summary: A board silkscreened LSM303 can carry a DLH, DLM, DLHC, D or AGR die. The AGR answers on exactly the same two addresses as the DLHC but puts its magnetometer output in a different register block, so a DLHC driver reads sound accelerometer values beside a mute compass.
facts: Probe the accelerometer at address 0x19 and read register 0x0F: an AGR returns 0x33, while a DLHC has no identity register there at all. That one read separates the two chips that share both addresses
On an AGR the magnetometer identity sits at register 0x4F returning 0x40, and its output starts at register 0x68 in X, Y, Z order, not at register 0x03 like the DLHC

On DLM and DLHC parts the output at registers 0x03 to 0x08 is ordered X, Z, Y, while on the DLH it is X, Y, Z, so reading six bytes in order swaps two axes and yields a heading that looks plausible and is wrong
An LSM303D returns 0x49 at register 0x0F, answers at a single address and puts its magnetometer data at register 0x08; it is not even pin compatible with the earlier carriers
DLH, DLM and DLHC all return the same identity triplet at registers 0x0A to 0x0C, so that triplet proves the link works and proves nothing about which of the three you hold

name: The GY-50 outline ships as L3G4200D, L3GD20 or L3GD20H
summary: Successor gyros moved the bus address, so a board sold under one module name simply does not answer where the older sketch looks. The identity register settles it in one read, and a popular driver actively refuses the older die.
facts: Read register 0x0F: 0xD3 is an L3G4200D, 0xD4 an L3GD20, 0xD7 an L3GD20H
The address blocks differ: an L3G4200D answers at 0x68 or 0x69 while the successors answer at 0x6A or 0x6B, so a scan finding nothing at 0x68 should look higher before wiring is blamed
A widely used Adafruit driver accepts only 0xD4 and 0xD7 and rejects an L3G4200D outright, while the Pololu library accepts all three and picks the address itself
Full scale wording shifts too, 250 degrees per second on the older part against 245 on the successors, so a hardcoded scaling constant is only approximate across the swap

name: The HMC6352 address printed everywhere is the eight-bit form
summary: The vendor documents the slave address as 0x42 to write and 0x43 to read, the eight-bit form with the direction bit already in place. Arduino takes seven-bit addresses, so the value that works is 0x21, and a scanner reporting 0x21 makes a beginner conclude the module is faulty.
aliases: heading in tenths of a degree
facts: Pass 0x21 to the wire library, which is 0x42 shifted right by one bit; both numbers describe the same chip
Run a scanner: a healthy part shows at 0x21 and nowhere else, so seeing 0x21 while every tutorial says 0x42 is the expected state, not a fault
The address lives in memory location 0x00 and is user changeable within 0x10 to 0xF6, so a second hand module can genuinely sit elsewhere and the scan is the only way to know
The part answers with a heading already computed in tenths of a degree from 0 to 3599, so dividing by ten is the whole conversion and no angle maths is needed

name: ITG-3200 boots in a reserved full scale and its scale factor does not apply
summary: The power-on value of the full scale field is zero, and the datasheet marks codes 0, 1 and 2 as reserved: only code 3 has a specified range and a specified scale factor. Readings still respond to motion, so nothing looks broken while every value in degrees per second is off by an unspecified factor.
facts: Write 0x18 to register 0x16: the datasheet says the reset value is zero and instructs to set the full scale field to 3 for proper operation
The 14.375 counts per degree per second that every tutorial divides by is specified only under that setting, so applied to a chip left at reset it has no stated meaning
Write 0x01 to register 0x3E: the power-up clock is the internal relaxation oscillator, and the datasheet highly recommends one of the gyros or an external clock instead, for stability
An integrated angle built on the reset clock drifts for a reason no amount of zero-rate calibration removes
Register 0 is not a fixed signature: it holds the bus address and is writable, so a matching value proves an address rather than a part

name: Digital potentiometers carry one milliamp and forget their setting
summary: The name digital potentiometer promises a knob you can command, and it is not one: the wiper is rated one milliamp, the lowest code is tens of ohms rather than zero, and the wiper snaps back to mid scale at every power-up.
aliases: rs pin returns to mid scale
facts: The wiper current is specified between minus and plus one milliamp, so driving a light, a motor or a speaker through the wiper is outside spec by an order of magnitude where a mechanical knob passes tens
Wiper resistance at the lowest code is 52 ohms typical and 100 maximum on the 10 kilohm parts, and 125 typical on the 50 kilohm parts, so turning it all the way down never reaches zero

The datasheet is explicit that the wiper resets to mid scale at power-up and that the reset pin does the same in hardware: the setting is volatile and any project surviving a power cycle must re-send it at boot
Reproducible check: set a distinctive code, cut power, restore it and read the divider. Mid rail means this family; the stored value means a different, non volatile family

name: ADS7830 channel numbers are interleaved in the command byte
summary: The die is genuine and in production; the trap is entirely in the command byte. Single-ended channel numbers are interleaved, so indexing them in order samples the wrong physical pin on six channels out of eight, with plausible values throughout.
facts: The reference library spells the interleaving out: channel 0 is command 0x08, channel 2 is 0x09, channel 4 is 0x0A, channel 6 is 0x0B, then channel 1 is 0x0C. Only channels 0 and 7 fall where naive indexing expects them
Asking for channel 1 by shifting the index actually samples physical channel 2, and asking for channel 2 samples channel 4
The internal reference defaults to OFF at power-up, so the PD1 bit must be set on every conversion when using it, and the first read after enabling it is invalid and should be discarded

The Adafruit breakout ties its reference pin to the supply, while its own library defaults to the internal reference ON, which the datasheet forbids in that configuration. Pass the external reference mode explicitly and scale by the supply, not by 2.5 volts
Address 0x48 identifies nothing here: an ADS1115 and a PCF8591 occupy the same address block, and one kit ships either part under one name

name: TSL2561 driver tests the revision nibble instead of the part number
summary: The die is genuine, but the reference driver identifies the part by masking the revision half of the identity register rather than the part-number half. It therefore refuses sound parts and welcomes dies of an entirely different family.
facts: The driver reads the identity register then tests it against mask 0x05, whose two bits both live inside the revision half, so the part number is never examined at all
A datasheet-conformant part reads 0x5R. Of the sixteen possible revisions twelve are refused by that mask, while 0x00 -- a different chip entirely -- passes
Real boards are reported returning 0x0A from that register across different years and vendors, so the refusal message names neither a wiring fault nor a counterfeit: check the library version first
An earlier attempt to fix this shipped an operator precedence slip and bricked previously sound boards, so pinning an older release is a real remedy
Saturation is the mirror image: the driver returns 65536 when the part is blinded, while its own shipped example tests for a reading of zero and prints an overload message in darkness instead

name: MMC5603 identity register reads zero and the driver accepts it
summary: The product identifier that should name the chip reads 0x00 on real parts, so the driver was patched to accept 0x00 and now reports success for almost any device at that address, including a different magnetometer that shares it.
aliases: data rate must be non zero
facts: Read the product identifier at register 0x39 yourself and log it: 0x10 confirms an MMC5603, while 0x00 is ambiguous and could be anything
An MMC5603 and an MMC5983MA both answer at address 0x30, so a bus scan separates nothing; read 0x39 expecting 0x10 and 0x2F expecting 0x30, and exactly one should match

Setting continuous mode without first setting a non zero data rate freezes the readings forever, because the chip refuses continuous mode at rate zero while the driver reports it as active from a software cache
Symptom of that: X, Y and Z identical on every read, and the temperature reading coming back as no number at all
The Adafruit breakout has X and Y swapped on its silkscreen, reported by two people and still open, so verify empirically which printed axis tracks north before writing any heading code

name: INA169 breakouts ship two shunt values a hundred apart
summary: Two vendors sell an INA169 board with the same chip and different sense resistors, 10 ohms against 0.1. Neither silkscreen says so, and the same sketch moved between them reports a current wrong by a factor of one hundred.
facts: The SparkFun board ships with a 10 ohm sense resistor giving a span of 3.5 to 35 milliamps, and its own example sketch hardcodes that value
The Adafruit board ships with a 0.1 ohm resistor scaled at one volt per amp up to 5 amps, which is exactly one hundred times apart
Reproducible check: draw a few hundred milliamps. If the output pins near the rail, the board carries the 10 ohm shunt
The vendor documents swapping it: 10 ohms for 3.5 to 35 milliamps, 1 ohm for 35 to 350, 0.1 ohm for 350 milliamps to 3.5 amps
Read the value off the board rather than assuming it from the part name, then apply the formula with that number

name: TMC2209 idles at one eighth step and has no full step mode
summary: Sold as an A4988-shaped drop-in, the TMC2209 does the opposite of an A4988 when its mode pins are grounded: it selects one eighth microstepping where the A4988 selects full step, so a motor commanded two hundred steps advances an eighth of a turn.
aliases: steps per mm eight times off
facts: The vendor configuration table shows both mode pins grounded selecting one eighth steps with interpolation, and there is NO combination that yields full step at all
The pins carry internal pull-downs, so leaving them unconnected also selects one eighth
The A4988 table gives full step for the same all-low combination, which is what makes the swap silently wrong: every commanded move comes out eight times too short
Enable the serial interface and those same two pins stop choosing microsteps entirely: they carry the slave address, bit 0 and bit 1, giving four addresses
Reproducible check: command exactly two hundred pulses on a 1.8 degree motor. Less than a full turn at the shaft confirms a microstepped mode

name: STSPIN220 has the A4988 footprint but dies above ten volts
summary: This carrier matches the A4988 in size, pinout and interface, so it drops into the same socket. Its motor supply tops out at ten volts where the A4988 accepts thirty-five, so the twelve volts a stepper normally runs on destroys it.
facts: Motor supply is specified from 1.8 to 10 volts, and the vendor steers higher voltage users to the STSPIN820, which runs from 7 to 45
The A4988 it physically replaces runs from 8 to 35 volts, so the two overlap only between 8 and 10 and the usual 12 or 24 volt supply is outside the range entirely
The vendor hedges its compatibility claim with phrases easy to miss: the pinout matches in most respects, and it drops in for many applications
Microstep selection is latched rather than static: two of the resolution inputs share pins with step and direction, and their values are read at power-up or when standby is released
Consequence: rewiring those pins while the driver runs changes nothing, because they are already acting as step and direction

name: The multiplexer bought to fix address clashes arrives in one
summary: The TCA9548A defaults to an address that a servo driver, a display backpack and a humidity part also answer. Worse, the servo driver replies there through its all-call address whatever its own is set to, so the clash cannot be fixed from that side.
aliases: channel select acknowledged by the wrong chip
facts: The multiplexer ships at address 0x70 and straps from 0x70 to 0x77 via its three address pins; pulling the first one high clears the clash
A public device directory lists eight parts at that address, including a display backpack, a servo driver and a humidity part

The servo driver case cannot be fixed by re-addressing it: its all-call address is enabled at power-up and every one of them acknowledges there until firmware disables it. The multiplexer is the part that must move
Symptom: a scan shows a device at 0x70 and the multiplexer seems to answer, but channel writes are acknowledged by the other chip, so nothing downstream ever appears
Sequence when a servo driver and a multiplexer share a bus: move the multiplexer first, confirm two separate addresses in a scan, then bring up the channels

name: GUVA-S12SD boards amplify the same photocurrent very differently
summary: The die outputs a photocurrent and every breakout wraps it in its own amplifier: 4.3 volts per microamp on one board, about six times that on another, and ten times more again on an older run of the same board. The index formula copied into every tutorial fits only one of them.
facts: One vendor board is a single stage at 4.3 volts per microamp, so one microamp of photocurrent gives 4.3 volts out
Another adds a second stage of about six times, so the same light gives roughly six times the reading, and an older run of that board used a ten times larger feedback resistor on the first stage
The two circulating index formulas both assume the low gain configuration, so on a two stage board the index is only valid after physically bypassing the second stage

Reproducible check: read the output in direct midday sun. A few hundred millivolts is the low gain build; a reading pinned near the supply is a high gain build and any index computed from it is meaningless

name: LPS28DFW halves its counts per hectopascal in the second range
summary: The part has two full scale ranges, and switching to the wider one changes the conversion constant from 4096 to 2048 counts per hectopascal. Code that keeps dividing by the first reports exactly half the true pressure, with no flag and a plausible number.
facts: Sensitivity is 4096 counts per hectopascal in the narrow range and 2048 in the wide one, so the divisor must follow the active mode
Signature symptom: a sea level reading near 506 rather than about 1013 hectopascals, an exact halving rather than drift or noise
The interrupt threshold register scales the same way, so a threshold ported between modes fires at the wrong pressure too
The default address is 0x5C with an alternate selectable by jumper, so a scan cannot tell a mis-scaled part from a sound one

name: SEN5x stays mute unless its select pin is grounded
summary: The module powers up in serial mode and speaks the two-wire bus only if its select pin is tied to ground, before or as it powers up. Wire the bus perfectly and the module stays absent from a scan, unexplained by anything printed on the board.
facts: Pin 5 is the interface select and must be pulled to ground to choose the two-wire bus; left floating the module answers only on the serial link
The grounding must happen before or at the moment of power-up: pulling it low afterwards leaves the module on the serial link, so power-cycle after wiring it
The module needs 5 volts on its supply, since the internal fan requires that rail to spin reliably, while its logic tolerates both levels

The three variants are pin identical and share the command set but measure different quantities: only the top one reports nitrogen oxides, and asking a lesser one returns an unavailable value rather than an error

name: The SHT15 clock and data pins are not an I2C bus
summary: The breakout exposes supply, ground, clock and data, so it gets wired to the I2C pins and driven with the standard library. The datasheet states the part cannot be addressed by I2C at all: a scanner will never list it, because it has no slave address.
facts: The datasheet says it outright: the sensor cannot be addressed by I2C, though it can share the wires without disturbing other devices. An empty scan is the EXPECTED result for a healthy part
The frame carries no address byte: a transmission start sequence, then three address bits of which only all-zero is supported, then five command bits
The data line needs an external pull-up around 10 kilohms, and the host must only ever drive it low, never high

After a measure command the host waits for the sensor to pull data low, up to 320 milliseconds at the finest resolution. Recovery is the vendor's own connection reset: hold data high and toggle the clock nine times or more
Self-heating budget: the part should be active under a tenth of the time, so about one measurement per second, or the readings run warm

name: An unpowered SHT25 pulls the bus lines to ground
summary: The datasheet states that with its supply at zero volts the clock and data pads are pulled to ground as well, blocking the bus. A loose supply wire, or switching the part off from a pin to save power, silently removes every OTHER device.
aliases: capteur non alimente bloque le bus
facts: The datasheet is explicit: with the supply set to zero volts the clock and data pads are pulled to ground too, and the bus is blocked for as long as that lasts

Diagnostic: if a scanner lists NOTHING at all after this part joined a previously sound bus, meter both lines. Near zero with pull-ups fitted means something is clamping them; unplug this part's supply and see whether the others reappear
This rules out the common trick of powering a part from a digital pin to sleep it: driving that supply low is exactly the blocking condition
Its address is fixed at 0x40 with no address pin, shared with a whole family, so two of them need a multiplexer and a scan cannot say which family member answered
Hold-master commands keep the clock low for the whole conversion, which some bus controllers time out on; the no-hold variants leave the bus free and are polled instead

name: The US-100 rear jumper switches it out of trigger and echo mode
summary: It looks and pins out like the common ultrasonic module, so it gets wired as one and driven with pulse timing. A shunt on the rear header selects the protocol: fitted, the module answers only on a serial link and the timing code waits forever.
facts: With the rear jumper removed it behaves like the classic module, trigger and echo. With the jumper fitted the same two pins carry a serial link at 9600 baud
On the serial link, send 0x55 and read two bytes giving the distance in millimetres, most significant first; send 0x50 for the temperature byte. No trigger pulse exists in that mode
Diagnostic without rewiring: hook a terminal at 9600 baud to the two signal pins and send 0x55. Two bytes back proves the jumper is fitted
Its echo output follows the supply rail rather than being fixed at five volts, so copying the divider wiring used for the classic module adds an error on a 3.3 volt board
It carries a temperature sensor and compensates the speed of sound, so a disagreement with the classic module as ambient changes is this part behaving correctly

name: A DRV8825 in an A4988 socket runs hotter at the same trimmer setting
summary: The carrier shares the footprint and control interface, so it is swapped in without touching the current trimmer. The two boards convert the reference voltage to coil current with different constants, and the pin that fed the older part its logic supply is now a fault output.
facts: On this carrier the current limit is simply the reference voltage times two, while the A4988 divides it by eight times its sense resistor
At an untouched reference of 0.80 volts that gives 1.60 amps here against 1.00 on a common A4988 clone, sixty percent more current into the same motor
The pin that supplied logic voltage on the A4988 is this part's fault output, since it needs no logic supply, so a board feeding it there is back-driving an open-drain pin
The current trimmer sits at a different end of the board, so orient by the labelled direction, ground, enable and motor pins, never by the trimmer position
Microstepping differs too, reaching one thirty-second where the older part stops at one sixteenth, so the same mode jumpers give a different step count

name: SIM800L wants 3.4 to 4.4 volts, so neither board rail feeds it
summary: The bare breakout has a supply pin like any module, but the specification is 3.4 to 4.4 volts: the five volt rail is over the maximum and the 3.3 volt rail is under the shutdown floor. Transmit bursts pull up to two amps.
aliases: buck converter set to four volts
facts: The vendor specifies 3.4 to 4.4 volts with 4.0 recommended, and states the module powers itself down outside that window. The five volt pin exceeds the maximum and the 3.3 volt pin is below the minimum
The transmitting burst causes a voltage drop and the supply must deliver up to two amps, which is why a switching converter is recommended over a linear regulator
Total impedance between a lithium cell and the supply pins must stay under 150 milliohms: long jumper wires and a breadboard rail already blow that budget, so an adequate battery still browns out

Reproducible check: watch the supply pin while the module registers on the network. A dip crossing 3.4 volts that coincides with the module going quiet is it powering itself down, rather than a firmware fault
Standard remedy: a two amp switching converter set to 4.0 volts plus a large bulk capacitor across the supply pins, physically close

name: The board 3.3 volt pin is rated 50 mA, the radio draws 170
summary: An ESP-01 wired to the board's 3.3 volt pin powers up and answers commands, then resets the instant the radio transmits. The chip is rated 170 milliamps typical transmitting, the pin 50 maximum: a shortfall of more than three times.
aliases: reset au moment de rejoindre le wifi
facts: The chip datasheet gives 170 milliamps typical while transmitting and about 50 receiving, while the board specification rates its 3.3 volt pin at 50 maximum

Signature symptom that separates this from a wiring fault: the module replies to commands while it merely receives, then cuts out on the first join or connect, which is the first moment the radio transmits at full power
Supply range runs from 2.5 to 3.6 volts, so the five volt rail sits outside the absolute maximum and the chip tolerates 3.6 at most
Its receive pin tops out at 3.6 volts too, so a five volt transmit line needs a level shifter independently of the supply question
The remedy is a separate regulator sized for the burst, around half an amp, with grounds tied together. A resistor divider off five volts collapses under a 170 milliamp step

name: WIZ820io runs a W5200, which the old Ethernet library cannot drive
summary: Bought as the compact stand-in for the classic Ethernet shield, this module carries a different controller with a different register layout. Every stock example compiles, and the begin call fails without saying why on any library older than 2.0.
facts: The controller inside is a W5200, not the W5100 of the classic shield, and the vendor lists the module as not recommended for new design with support ended
The check that settles which controller is present: the W5200 has a version register at 0x001F reading 0x03. The W5100 has no version register at all, and the W5500 keeps its at 0x0039 reading 0x04
The Arduino library only gained automatic detection of the three controllers in version 2.0.0, so anything older drives the W5100 exclusively: check the library version before re-checking the wiring
The module is 3.3 volt only, with no regulator or level translation on board, so both power and the serial bus must be handled at that level
The successor in the same footprint carries a W5500, so migrating is a controller and library change rather than a re-layout

name: The TMP102 half-degree figure is typical, the guarantee is two
summary: The front page of the datasheet advertises half a degree without calibration, and that number is copied into every listing. In the electrical table it sits in the typical column: the guaranteed maximum is two degrees over the useful range.
aliases: ecart d un degre au thermometre
facts: The electrical table gives half a degree typical and TWO degrees maximum between minus twenty-five and eighty-five, and one typical against three maximum over the full range. A part reading one and a half degrees off a reference is inside specification
The vendor's own comparison table lists the TMP112 at half a degree MAXIMUM in the same pin-compatible package: if the guarantee is what you need, the part number is wrong rather than the wiring
