Resolution is not accuracy: one step is 0.0625 degrees, so the reading shows four convincing digits wrapped around a two degree guarantee
Supply is 1.4 to 3.6 volts, so the five volt rail is over the absolute maximum, while the open-drain bus itself needs no level shifter
While debugging a suspicious value, read the mode bit of the second temperature byte: it says whether the part is in twelve or thirteen bit alignment, so the shift can be checked rather than assumed

name: TMP006 returns a thermopile voltage, not an object temperature
summary: The part has no object temperature register. It gives a raw thermopile voltage and a die temperature, and the object figure is a polynomial whose leading constant belongs to each individual sensor and its window. Every board ships one hardcoded value.
facts: The library reads exactly two registers, the thermopile voltage and the die temperature, and computes the rest in software from constants that are identical on every board sold
The vendor guide says the leading constant is found by a two-point calibration, meaning per assembled system: a shared literal is a placeholder, and no averaging in the sketch improves it

Default coefficients assume a black body of emissivity 0.95 and a 110 degree field of view; the vendor guideline is to use it only above 0.7, so polished metal is out of range while the part still returns a confident number
That field of view means a cone average rather than a spot: at ten centimetres it averages a patch roughly twenty-eight across, so aiming at a small object mostly measures its background
The maker declared the family end-of-life citing the complexity of system calibration for its customers, with no replacement planned

name: The SI1145 has no ultraviolet photodiode at all
summary: Sold as a digital ultraviolet index part, it contains no ultraviolet sensing element: the index is computed from its visible and infrared channels using solar coefficients. Away from direct sun the number is an extrapolation with no ultraviolet content behind it.
facts: The vendor states it plainly: the part contains no actual ultraviolet sensing element and approximates the index from visible and infrared light from the sun

Reproducible check: the reported index rises under an incandescent lamp, which has strong infrared and no ultraviolet, and collapses in sun behind infrared-blocking glazing, where real ultraviolet is present. A true ultraviolet photodiode behaves the opposite way in both tests

The derivation rests on four coefficient registers holding factory constants tuned for a solar spectrum, and the maker revised the recommended defaults at a later datasheet revision, so two drivers calibrate identical hardware differently
The visible and infrared channels are real measurements and remain trustworthy; only the index is derived
Both order codes are obsolete and the breakout is discontinued, so a board in a drawer is old stock that no library update will change

name: The HDC3021 ships with protective tape over its element
summary: It leaves the factory with tape bonded over the humidity element to survive reflow and washing, and boards ship with it still attached. Its successor carries a white filter that must STAY on, so one guide carries two opposite instructions.
facts: The vendor warns that the part comes with a protective sticker on top which must be removed before use; the board arrives with it on, and neither the part number nor the silkscreen mentions it

The maker gives the reason and the obligation: the tape shields the element from manufacturing pollutants and must be removed after the final stages of assembly for accurate readings. It survives three reflow cycles, which is why it is still there

Symptom is a half-measuring part: temperature tracks a reference correctly while relative humidity sits near a fixed value and barely moves when you breathe on the board. Look at the element under a light before suspecting the bus or the driver
Removal technique matters because the element scratches: grip the adhesive-free tab at a corner with tweezers and peel diagonally upward rather than sliding across the surface
The opposite rule applies to the successor sold on the same listing: an amber clear tape is peeled off, a white porous disc is left alone

name: The HDC1080 that replaces the HDC1008 loses its address pins
summary: The older part is end of life, and the one people buy instead is no drop-in twin: it has no address-select pins, so it is stuck at one address, and it answers the identity check with a different value that older drivers refuse.
aliases: deux capteurs sur un seul bus
facts: The older part has two address-select pins giving four addresses, so up to four share one bus. The newer one has none and is fixed at a single address, so a two-part design needs a multiplexer after the swap
The identity check moved: the value reported by the identity register changed from 0x1000 to 0x1050 with the newer family, and older drivers refuse anything outside their accepted list

Diagnostic for the confusing case, where a scanner finds a device but the driver reports nothing there: read the maker identity register, which must give 0x5449, then the device identity. A value of 0x1050 with a refusing driver means the library is too old
The maker marks the older part as end of life while keeping it available to existing customers

name: The Si4713 answers nothing until a pin toggles its reset line
summary: The transmitter stays silent on the bus until its reset line has been driven low and back high by a microcontroller pin, so a scan at power-up returns an empty bus and the board seems absent. Its address is strapped rather than fixed.
aliases: reset a basculer avant tout dialogue
facts: The vendor is explicit: the reset pin must toggle before you start communicating with the chip. Leaving it unconnected yields an empty scan with no message
Correct order: drive reset low, brief delay, drive it high, brief delay, and only then start the bus or run the scanner
The address is strapped rather than fixed: pulled high by default it answers at 0x63, shorted to ground it answers at 0x11, so a stray solder bridge relocates it
Diagnostic: scan once before pulsing reset and once after. An empty result before and a device after confirms a sound board and a missing reset

name: The DS3502 wakes in the mode where every wiper write burns memory
summary: Its control register is volatile and comes up cleared, which puts the part in the mode where a wiper write is also programmed into nonvolatile memory. A driver that skips the mode bit turns a fade into tens of thousands of writes, and the part degrades gradually.
aliases: mode bit du registre de controle
facts: Two registers decide it: the wiper at 0x00 and the control register at 0x02, whose top bit selects volatile-only writes. With that bit clear, every wiper write is also programmed into nonvolatile memory
The control register is volatile and powers up cleared, so the memory-writing mode is active on every single power-up, and the board gives no sign of it

Endurance is rated and finite: a minimum of fifty thousand writes at 70 degrees. A sweep of a hundred and twenty-eight steps is one write per step, so a sustained fade reaches the rating in minutes, and the decline is gradual rather than a clean error
The vendor drivers already guard this by writing the top bit at initialisation, yet neither documents why, so a hand-rolled driver omits it silently
Diagnostic: after your driver initialises, read back the control register. A cleared value means every wiper update is being burned in

name: The five-volt-ready ADXL335 board never swings near five volts
summary: The board takes five volts in and regulates them to 3.3, and the outputs are ratiometric to that lower rail, so on a five-volt-referenced converter zero gravity lands nowhere near mid-scale. The product page also overstates the span.
facts: Reproducible bench check with the stock five volt reference and a ten-bit converter: lay the board flat and still. Two axes should read about 338 counts and the vertical one about 405. A sketch assuming 512 means zero carries a constant offset near 2.6 g
The outputs are ratiometric to the regulated 3.3 volts, so zero gravity sits at 1.65 volts rather than half of five

The datasheet contradicts the product page on the span: at 3.3 volts sensitivity is about 330 millivolts per g, so plus or minus three g occupies 0.66 to 2.64 volts rather than the full rail. Mapping the whole rail under-reads by about 1.67 times, and mapping five volts by 2.5
With the five volt reference the whole range occupies about 406 of 1024 counts, so sixty percent of the converter is thrown away for nothing

Fix: feed the board's own 3.3 volt output to the reference pin and select the external reference. Do it BEFORE the first analog read, or the internal and external references are shorted together and the microcontroller can be damaged

name: The GY-33 hides its TCS34725 behind an onboard microcontroller
summary: Sold under the name of the colour chip it carries, this board interposes its own microcontroller: it answers at 0x5A while the bare chip sits at 0x29, unreachable from outside. A driver written for the chip therefore addresses an empty slot.
aliases: mode uart selectionne sur la carte
adafruit tcs34725 finds an empty address
facts: The board carries its own microcontroller between the host bus and the colour chip, so what answers on the bus is that microcontroller, and the TCS34725 stays behind it
Addresses are the visible signature: this board answers at 0x5A, while a transparent TCS34725 breakout answers at 0x29
Reproducible check: run a bus scan. A device at 0x5A with silence at 0x29 identifies this board; a transparent breakout shows exactly the reverse
Consequence for the driver: a library written for the bare chip talks to 0x29, reports an absent device, and the message reads as a wiring fault when the wiring is sound

The board also offers a serial interface, selected on the board itself, and a dedicated library exists for it precisely because the chip's own library cannot drive it -- the existence of a board-specific library IS the warning sign
Public reports show the raw chip address never appearing in a scan of this board, which is what an interposed controller produces

name: A black MH-Z19B board is an imitation, and its CO2 reads LOW
summary: Winsen builds this CO2 module on a GREEN board. Imitations use a black one, and they under-report ppm -- the dangerous direction, since a room that needs airing then reads as acceptable. The giveaway is visible before any code runs.
facts: Board colour is the first check and it costs nothing: a genuine MH-Z19B is GREEN, and a BLACK pcb is the sign reported across an entire specialist review of these CO2 imitations
Housing differs too: the genuine casing carries raised contours and embossed texturing, while the imitation is completely smooth and often slightly yellowish, and it lacks the RoHS marking
Measured side by side in one published comparison, genuine units read about 2400 to 2600 ppm while an imitation read 1500 ppm in the same air. The error runs LOW, so poor air quality reads as fine
Imitations ship with the wrong cable, and the pin labels printed on them disagree with the real arrangement, so verify the pinout against Winsen documentation BEFORE applying power

⚠️ Two claims often repeated about these imitations were checked on 2026-08-27 and appear on NO source that could be opened: a 10000 ppm range reported at startup, and a calibration constant of 436 in place of 410. Rely on the visible signs above; treat those two as rumour

name: The MCP23S17 shares the MCP23017 pinout and speaks SPI, never I2C
summary: One letter separates two chips that share a package, a pinout and a register map. The MCP23017 speaks I2C; the MCP23S17 speaks SPI only. Put an MCP23S17 on an I2C bus and the scan stays empty, which looks like a wiring mistake and is none.
aliases: expandeur de broches muet sur i2c

i2c scanner empty for a port expander
facts: Microchip documents both chips in a SINGLE datasheet and states the difference in one line: they differ only in the serial interface, I2C for the MCP23017 and SPI for the MCP23S17. Same 28-pin package, same register map, same 16 gpio lines
The one visible difference on the board is pin 11: chip select on the SPI part, left unconnected on the I2C part
Consequence, and it is total: an MCP23S17 answers NOTHING on I2C. The scan finds an empty bus, which looks exactly like a missing pull-up or a swapped SDA and SCL pair
Diagnostic that settles it in ten seconds: read the marking printed on the chip itself. An S between 23 and 17 means the SPI variant, and rewiring I2C will never help
Three address straps give 0x20 through 0x27 on the I2C part, so an empty scan across that WHOLE block points at the chip rather than at one address
